claim: Natural Killer (NK) cells are essential for control of viral infection and cancer.
source: Natural Killer (NK) cells are essential for control of viral infection and cancer.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations in the manuscript (Raulet and Guerra, 2009; Lodoen and Lanier, 2006).

claim: NK cells express NKG2D, an activating receptor that directly recognizes NKG2D ligands.
source: NK cells express NKG2D, an activating receptor that directly recognizes NKG2D ligands.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about NK cell biology.

claim: NKG2D ligands are expressed at low level on healthy cells, but are induced by stresses like infection and transformation.
source: These are expressed at low level on healthy cells, but are induced by stresses like infection and transformation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NKG2D ligand expression patterns.

claim: The mouse cytomegalovirus encoded protein m18 is necessary and sufficient to drive expression of the RAE-1 family of NKG2D ligands.
source: We observed that the mouse cytomegalovirus encoded protein m18 is necessary and sufficient to drive expression of the RAE-1 family of NKG2D ligands.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: RAE-1 is transcriptionally repressed by histone deacetylase inhibitor 3 (HDAC3) in healthy cells.
source: We demonstrate that RAE-1 is transcriptionally repressed by histone deacetylase inhibitor 3 (HDAC3) in healthy cells
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing HDAC3-specific inhibitors induce RAE-1 expression.

claim: m18 relieves HDAC3-mediated repression by directly interacting with Casein Kinase II and preventing it from activating HDAC3.
source: m18 relieves this repression by directly interacting with Casein Kinase II and preventing it from activating HDAC3.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data showing m18-CK2 interaction and immunofluorescence data showing reduced HDAC3 phosphorylation.

claim: HDAC inhibiting proteins from human herpesviruses induce human NKG2D ligand ULBP-1.
source: Accordingly, we found that HDAC inhibiting proteins from human herpesviruses induce human NKG2D ligand ULBP-1.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 9 showing IE1 and ICP0 induce ULBP-1.

claim: Virally mediated HDAC inhibition can act as a signal for the host to activate NK-cell recognition.
source: Thus our findings indicate that virally mediated HDAC inhibition can act as a signal for the host to activate NK-cell recognition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings showing viral HDAC inhibitors induce NKG2D ligands.

claim: NK cells recognize and lyse cells undergoing infection or transformation.
source: NK cells recognize and lyse cells undergoing infection or transformation as well as secrete pro-inflammatory molecules that activate the adaptive immune system (Smyth et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: NKG2D is expressed on NK cells, NK T cells, γδT cells, and CD8 and CD4 T cells.
source: The activating receptor NKG2D is expressed on NK cells and provides one mechanism by which NK cells (as well as NK T cells, γδT cells, and CD8 and CD4 T cells) recognize their targets (Raulet, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: NKG2D surveillance protects mice from several models of induced or spontaneous cancer.
source: NKG2D surveillance protects mice from several models of induced or spontaneous cancer (Smyth et al., 2005b; Guerra et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A polymorphism predicted to reduce NKG2D signaling is linked to both increased cancer risk and susceptibility to viral infections in humans.
source: In humans, a polymorphism predicted to reduce NKG2D signaling is linked to both increased cancer risk (Roszak et al., 2012) and susceptibility to viral infections (Taniguchi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to human genetic studies.

claim: In humans, NKG2D ligands include two families: ULBP1-6 and MICA-B.
source: The ligands for NKG2D are diverse, and include two families in humans (ULBP1-6 and MICA-B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about human NKG2D ligands.

claim: In mice, the ULBP family is subdivided into RAE-1α-ε, MULT-1, and H60a-c subfamilies.
source: In mice, the MICA-B family is not represented and the ULBP family is subdivided into RAE-1α-ε, MULT-1, and H60a-c subfamilies (Raulet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Expression of a single NKG2D ligand family member is sufficient to stimulate killing by NK cells.
source: Each of these ligands binds NKG2D with a different affinity, but expression of a single family member is sufficient to stimulate killing by NK cells (Champsaur and Lanier, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Silencing of ULBP-1 by histone deacetylases (HDACs) has been shown by López-Soto and colleagues.
source: It is still not well understood how the majority of NKG2D ligands are silenced in healthy tissue, but work by López-Soto and colleagues have shown that silencing by histone deacetylases (HDACs) is involved, at least for ULBP-1 (López-Soto et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: DNA damage leads to NKG2D ligand expression.
source: In this regard, several stimuli leading to ligand expression have been identified, these include: DNA damage (Gasser et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Hyper-proliferation through the transcription factor E2F leads to NKG2D ligand expression.
source: hyper-proliferation (though the transcription factor E2F) (Jung et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: PI3K/Ras signaling leads to NKG2D ligand expression.
source: and PI3K/Ras signaling (Tokuyama et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Over 90% of the population is infected with one or more herpesviruses.
source: Over 90% of the population is infected with one or more of these double stranded DNA viruses (Wald and Corey, 2007; Staras et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Herpesvirus infection causes a transcriptional upregulation of NKG2D ligand expression.
source: Herpesvirus infection causes a transcriptional upregulation of NKG2D ligand expression (Lodoen et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Herpesviruses apply multiple strategies to avoid NKG2D recognition by reducing NKG2D ligand expression at the surface of infected cells.
source: yet these viruses apply multiple strategies to avoid NKG2D recognition by reducing NKG2D ligand expression at the surface of infected cells (Reviewed in Jonjić et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Hosts deficient in NK cell responses are especially prone to pathogenic herpesvirus infection.
source: Hosts deficient in NK cell responses, including those with mutations that are predicted to specifically reduce NKG2D signaling, are especially prone to pathogenic herpesvirus infection (Taniguchi et al., 2015; Biron et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Growth of herpesviruses with a defect in NKG2D ligand evasion are attenuated in vivo.
source: Conversely, growth of herpesviruses with a defect NKG2D ligand evasion are attenuated in vivo (Jonjić et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: PI3K signaling is required for NKG2D ligand expression in transformed cells as well as during MCMV infection.
source: For example, Phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) signaling is required for NKG2D ligand expression in transformed cells as well as during mouse cytomegalovirus (MCMV) infection (Tokuyama et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: DNA damage signaling can mediate NKG2D ligand induction in both cancer development and KSHV infection.
source: Furthermore, DNA damage signaling can mediate NKG2D ligand induction in both cancer development (Gasser et al., 2005) and Kaposi's sarcoma herpesvirus (KSHV) infection (Bekerman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MCMV gene expression is necessary to induce RAE-1 expression during infection.
source: Previously, we showed that MCMV gene expression was necessary to induce RAE-1 expression during infection (Tokuyama et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: MCMV mutant virus deleted for ORFs m01 through m22 (∆m1-22) failed to induce Raet1 expression.
source: In contrast to WT MCMV or other mutant viruses, the MCMV mutant virus deleted for open reading frames (ORFs) m01 through m22 (∆m1-22) failed to induce Raet1 expression (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Levels of MCMV ie1 were comparable to WT virus in ∆m1-22 infected cells.
source: Levels of MCMV ie1 were comparable to WT virus (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A viral gene or combination of genes in the m01-m22 region is required to induce Raet1 expression.
source: These results indicate that a viral gene or a combination of genes in this region is required to induce Raet1 expression.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing ∆m1-22 fails to induce Raet1.

claim: Viruses lacking ORFs m12 to m18 (∆12–18) failed to induce Raet1 expression.
source: Viruses lacking ORFs m12 to m18 (∆12–18) and m18 to m22 (∆18–22) failed to induce Raet1 expression in contrast to WT MCMV (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Viruses lacking ORFs m18 to m22 (∆18–22) failed to induce Raet1 expression.
source: Viruses lacking ORFs m12 to m18 (∆12–18) and m18 to m22 (∆18–22) failed to induce Raet1 expression in contrast to WT MCMV (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Only MCMV lacking ORF m18 or ORF m19 failed to induce Raet1 expression.
source: Only MCMV lacking ORF m18 or ORF m19 failed to induce Raet1 expression (Figure 1D), indicating that one or both of these ORFs are required to induce Raet1 expression.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Expression of m18, but not m19 or vector control, rescued Raet1 expression in cells infected with mutant MCMV.
source: Expression of m18, but not m19 or vector control, rescued Raet1 expression in all cases Figure 1E,F) indicating that m18 is required for MCMV mediated Raet1 induction.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: Expression of m18 but not m19 was sufficient to induce Raet1 transcript.
source: Expression of m18 but not m19 was sufficient to induce Raet1 transcript and RAE-1 protein expression.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2A and flow cytometry data in Figure 2B.

claim: Expression of m18 but not m19 was sufficient to induce RAE-1 protein expression.
source: Expression of m18 but not m19 was sufficient to induce Raet1 transcript and RAE-1 protein expression.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2B.

claim: m18 is both necessary and sufficient to drive RAE-1 expression.
source: Thus, our data indicate that m18 is the both necessary and sufficient to drive RAE-1 expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: WT NK cells lysed m18-expressing fibroblasts in an NKG2D dependent manner.
source: We observed that WT NK cells lysed m18-expressing fibroblasts in an NKG2D dependent manner (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by chromium release assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A CTL epitope is produced from the m18 ORF.
source: Previous studies have identified a CTL epitope produced from the m18 ORF (Holtappels et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Peptides that correspond to the m18 ORF have been identified in mass spectrometric analysis of MCMV virions.
source: and peptides that correspond to this ORF have been identified in mass spectrometric analysis of MCMV virions (Kattenhorn et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: m18 mRNA is produced as early as 2 hr post-infection.
source: In accordance with previous studies we observed this was mRNA produced as early as 2 hr post-infection (Figure 2D) (Lacaze et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by semi-quantitative PCR data in Figure 2D and citation to previous work.

claim: m18 protein appears at a size of ~180 KDa on western blot, well above the predicted size of 110 KDa.
source: We observed a band at a size of ~180 KDa, well above the predicted size of 110 KDa, suggesting m18 is post-translationally modified.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 2E.

claim: m18 is post-translationally modified.
source: We observed a band at a size of ~180 KDa, well above the predicted size of 110 KDa, suggesting m18 is post-translationally modified.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between predicted and observed molecular weight.

claim: The m18-GFP fusion protein localized mostly to the nucleus.
source: We found that the m18-GFP fusion protein localized mostly to the nucleus (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 2F.

claim: Both m18-HA and m18-GFP constructs induced expression of RAE-1 similarly to other m18 constructs.
source: Importantly both m18-HA and m18-GFP constructs still induced expression of RAE-1 similarly to other m18 constructs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Co-expression of m18 increased the activity of the Raet1e promoter relative to vector control.
source: Co-expression of m18 increased the activity of the Raet1e promoter relative to vector control (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 3B.

claim: E2F sites in the Raet1e promoter are dispensable for activation of the Raet1e promoter by m18.
source: Although E2F sites in the Raet1e promoter have been shown to drive RAE-1 expression during proliferation (Jung et al., 2012), these sites were dispensable for activation of the Raet1e promoter by m18 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Promoter activation by m18 was eliminated when 25 nucleotides were deleted from the 5' end of the Raet1e promoter.
source: Promoters lacking 15 nucleotides at the 5' end of the promoter retained WT levels of induction in the presence of m18, but promoter activation by m18 was eliminated when 25 nucleotides were deleted (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 3B.

claim: The Raet1e promoter contains an m18 response element (m18RE) between −95 and −85 bp from the transcription start site.
source: These data indicate that the Raet1e promoter contains an m18 response element (m18RE) between −95 and −85 bp from the transcription start site.
evidence: This is inferred from the deletion mapping data in Figure 3B.

claim: The m18RE contains a Specificity factor transcription factor family (Sp TF) binding site.
source: Analysis of the m18RE for transcription factor (TF) binding sites using the JASPAR TF binding database (Mathelier et al., 2014) indicated a Specificity factor transcription factor family (Sp TF) binding site (Figure 3C) within the m18RE.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis using the JASPAR database.

claim: Promoter containing m18RE* showed significantly less promoter activity in the presence of m18 than the WT Raet1e promoter.
source: Promoter containing m18RE* showed significantly less promoter activity in the presence of m18 than the WT Raet1e promoter (Figure 3D), suggesting a role for Sp TFs in RAE-1 induction by m18.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 3D.

claim: Sp transcription factors bind to the m18RE.
source: Thus, the Sp consensus and m18RE oligos bind the same factors in nuclear lysate, suggesting that Sp TFs regulate Raet1 transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from EMSA competition assay data in Figure 3E.

claim: Sp3 occupies the Raet1e promoter.
source: Samples immunoprecipitated using an antibody against Sp3 but not Sp1 showed significant enrichment of the Raet1e promoter over the IgG control, indicating that Sp3 occupies the Raet1e promoter.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data in Figure 3F.

claim: m18 expression did not alter the amount of Sp3 bound to the Raet1e promoter.
source: Interestingly, m18 expression did not alter the amount of Sp3 bound to the Raet1e promoter (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data in Figure 3F (note: text says 3G but likely refers to 3F).

claim: Sp3 constitutively occupies the Raet1e promoter.
source: This indicates that Sp3 constitutively occupies the Raet1e promoter.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP data showing Sp3 binding regardless of m18 expression.

claim: Co-expression of DN-Sp and m18 resulted in a decreased percentage of RAE-1 expressing cells.
source: Co-expression of DN-Sp and m18 resulted in a decreased percentage of RAE-1 expressing cells (Figure 3G) suggesting that Sp factors are important for m18 to drive RAE-1 expression.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3G.

claim: Mithramycin treatment reduced RAE-1 induction by m18.
source: Mithramycin treatment reduced RAE-1 induction by m18 (Figure 3H) further indicating that Sp TF activity is required for RAE-1 induction by m18.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 3H.

claim: The human NKG2D ligand ULBP-1 is repressed by HDAC3 in the absence of stress.
source: The human NKG2D ligand ULBP-1 is repressed by histone deacetylase 3 (HDAC3) in the absence of stress.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work by López-Soto et al., 2009.

claim: HDAC3 is recruited to the ULBP1 promoter by Sp3.
source: HDAC3 is recruited to the ULBP1 promoter by Sp3 (López-Soto et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: HDAC inhibition induces RAE-1 expression.
source: Additionally, HDAC inhibition induces RAE-1 expression (Gasser et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The chemical HDAC inhibitor butyrate activated the WT Raet1e promoter.
source: Consistent with these findings, we observed that the chemical HDAC inhibitor butyrate activated the WT Raet1e promoter (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 4A.

claim: Butyrate treatment failed to drive expression from the m18RE* mutant Raet1e promoter.
source: Interestingly, butyrate treatment failed to drive expression from the m18RE* mutant Raet1e promoter (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 4A.

claim: Mithramycin treatment reduced RAE-1 expression in response to butyrate treatment.
source: Mithramycin treatment reduced RAE-1 expression in response to butyrate treatment (Figure 4B), indicating that Sp TFs are also required to drive RAE-1 expression in response to HDAC inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4B.

claim: The pan-HDAC inhibitors TSA and NaB induced RAE-1 expression.
source: The pan-HDAC inhibitors TSA and NaB induced RAE-1 expression, as did the HDAC1/3 inhibitor MS-275 and the HDAC3 inhibitor RGFP966.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4C.

claim: The HDAC1/3 inhibitor MS-275 induced RAE-1 expression.
source: The pan-HDAC inhibitors TSA and NaB induced RAE-1 expression, as did the HDAC1/3 inhibitor MS-275 and the HDAC3 inhibitor RGFP966.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4C.

claim: The HDAC3 inhibitor RGFP966 induced RAE-1 expression.
source: The pan-HDAC inhibitors TSA and NaB induced RAE-1 expression, as did the HDAC1/3 inhibitor MS-275 and the HDAC3 inhibitor RGFP966.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4C.

claim: An HDAC1 inhibitor did not induce RAE-1 expression.
source: In contrast, an HDAC1 inhibitor (4-(dimethylamino)-N-[6-(hydroxyamino)−6-oxohexyl]-benzamide), and an HDAC6,8 inhibitor (droxinostat) did not (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4C.

claim: An HDAC6,8 inhibitor (droxinostat) did not induce RAE-1 expression.
source: In contrast, an HDAC1 inhibitor (4-(dimethylamino)-N-[6-(hydroxyamino)−6-oxohexyl]-benzamide), and an HDAC6,8 inhibitor (droxinostat) did not (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 4C.

claim: HDAC3 is involved in RAE-1 repression.
source: These results indicate that HDAC3 is involved in RAE-1 repression, likely through recruitment to the promoter by Sp3 (López-Soto et al., 2009) though additional HDACs may be involved.
evidence: This is inferred from the HDAC inhibitor data and supported by citation.

claim: AcH3 levels were increased in m18 expressing mouse fibroblasts, as compared to those expressing vector control.
source: AcH3 levels were increased in m18 expressing mouse fibroblasts, as compared to those expressing vector control.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 5A.

claim: H3 levels were unchanged in m18 expressing mouse fibroblasts compared to vector control.
source: H3 levels were unchanged (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 5A.

claim: m18 expressing cells have significantly higher levels of AcH3 compared to non-transfected cells.
source: We compared the fluorescent intensity of AcH3 staining in the nucleus of m18 expressing cells, to non-transfected cells in the same field of view, and found significantly higher levels of AcH3 in m18 expressing cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: AcH3 level was unchanged in cells transfected with RFP alone.
source: AcH3 level was unchanged in cells transfected with RFP alone (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5C.

claim: Expression of m18-RFP or RFP alone did not affect H3 levels.
source: Expression of m18-RFP or RFP alone did not affect H3 levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: m18 expression increased acetylation at the Raet1e promoter.
source: Analysis of Raet1e promoter enrichment showed an increase in AcH3 levels associated with the Raet1e promoter in m18 expressing cells while H3 levels were unchanged (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data in Figure 5D.

claim: m18 increases histone acetylation in cells, including at the Raet1e promoter.
source: Together, these results indicate that m18 increases histone acetylation in cells, including at the Raet1e promoter.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 5.

claim: The most specific interaction identified by APMS was casein kinase II beta (CSNK2B).
source: This allowed identification of the most specific interaction as casein kinase II beta (CSNK2B) in APMS samples from human HEK293T cells.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data and Z-score analysis.

claim: The interaction between m18 and CK2 was confirmed in NIH-3T3 by IP-Western blot.
source: We confirmed the interaction with CK2 in NIH-3T3 by IP-Western blot (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by IP-Western blot data in Figure 6A.

claim: CK2 is involved in DNA damage signaling.
source: CK2 is involved in many biological processes, including DNA damage signaling (Ghavidel and Schultz, 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CK2 is involved in apoptosis.
source: apoptosis (Hellwig et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CK2 is involved in cell cycle progression.
source: and cell cycle progression (Homma and Homma, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CK2 is a constitutively active kinase that phosphorylates HDAC3 at serine 424 (S424) activating it.
source: CK2 is a constitutively active kinase that phosphorylates HDAC3 at serine 424 (S424) activating it (Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The activation of HDAC3 by CK2 has been demonstrated to help drive chromatin condensation during mitosis.
source: The activation of HDAC3 by CK2 has previously been demonstrated to help drive chromatin condensation during mitosis (Patil et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CK2 activation of HDAC3 has been shown to repress expression of genes during beige fat thermogenesis.
source: and has been shown to repress expression of genes during beige fat thermogenesis (Shinoda et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: TBBt treatment induced RAE-1 expression in excess of zVAD alone.
source: TBBt treatment induced RAE-1 expression in excess of zVAD alone (Figure 6D), indicating CK2 is a negative regulator of RAE-1 expression.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6B (note: text says 6D but likely refers to 6B).

claim: CK2 is a negative regulator of RAE-1 expression.
source: TBBt treatment induced RAE-1 expression in excess of zVAD alone (Figure 6D), indicating CK2 is a negative regulator of RAE-1 expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the CK2 inhibitor data.

claim: m18 expressing cells have significantly lower levels of HDAC3 S424 phosphorylation compared to non-transfected cells.
source: We compared the fluorescent intensity of HDAC3 S424 staining in the nucleus of m18 expressing cells, to non-transfected cells in the same field of view, and found significantly higher levels of HDAC3 S424 in m18 expressing cells (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 6C and 6D (note: text says 6F but likely refers to 6D).

claim: Overall levels of HDAC3 were unaffected by m18 transfection.
source: By the same measure overall levels of HDAC3 were unaffected by m18 transfection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The decrease in HDAC3 S424 phosphorylation was not observed in mouse fibroblasts transfected with control RFP vector.
source: This decrease was not observed in mouse fibroblasts transfected with control RFP vector.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6D.

claim: m18 inhibits HDAC3 activity by binding to CK2 and reducing HDAC3 phosphorylation.
source: Together, these results indicate that m18 inhibits HDAC3 activity by binding to CK2 and reducing HDAC3 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: The m18 ORF is highly conserved across strains of MCMV.
source: The fact that m18 ORF is highly conserved across strains of MCMV (Khairallah et al., 2015) suggests that m18 exert an essential function in MCMV life cycle.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: ∆18 MCMV did not grow significantly different from WT MCMV in vitro.
source: ∆18 MCMV did not grow significantly different from WT MCMV in this assay (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by plaque assay data in Figure 7A.

claim: MCMVm18stop fails to induce RAE-1 expression in mouse fibroblasts.
source: Like ∆18 MCMV, MCMVm18stop fails to induce RAE-1 expression in mouse fibroblasts, but has no defect in IE-1 expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: MCMVm18stop has no defect in IE-1 expression.
source: Like ∆18 MCMV, MCMVm18stop fails to induce RAE-1 expression in mouse fibroblasts, but has no defect in IE-1 expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mice infected with WT or MCMVm18stop had identical levels of MCMV in all organs assayed at five days post-infection.
source: Mice infected with WT or MCMVm18stop had identical levels of MCMV in all organs assayed at this time (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 7B.

claim: m18 elimination has no impact on viral growth in WT mice.
source: This indicates that m18 elimination has no impact on viral growth in WT mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vivo data in Figure 7B.

claim: RAG-/- yC-/- mice showed identical levels of MCMV between the WT and mutant viruses in spleen, lung, and liver.
source: Interestingly, these mice also showed identical levels of MCMV between the WT and mutant viruses in spleen, lung, and liver (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 7C.

claim: m18 is dispensable for viral growth at early time points in vivo.
source: Indicating that m18 is dispensable for viral growth at this early time point.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vivo data in Figure 7C.

claim: IE1 from HCMV is an HDAC inhibiting viral protein.
source: Two prominent examples of HDAC inhibiting viral proteins are IE1 from HCMV (Nevels et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: ICP0 from HSV-1 is an HDAC inhibiting viral protein.
source: and ICP0 from HSV-1 (Gu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Both ICP0 and IE1 induced expression of human ULBP1.
source: Both ICP0 and IE1 induced expression of human ULBP1 (Figure 9A, B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data in Figures 9A and 9B.

claim: Viral inhibition of HDACs is a common mechanism driving NKG2D ligand induction in humans and mice.
source: These results suggest that viral inhibition of HDACs is a common mechanism driving NKG2D ligand induction in humans and mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing multiple viral HDAC inhibitors induce NKG2D ligands.

claim: RAE-1 expression is repressed in the absence of stress signals due to closed chromatin around the Raet1 locus.
source: Our results suggest a model in which RAE-1 expression is repressed in the absence of stress signals due to closed chromatin around the Raet1 locus.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: Repression of RAE-1 is maintained by constitutive phosphorylation and activation of HDAC3 by CK2.
source: This repression is maintained by constitutive phosphorylation and activation of HDAC3 by CK2.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: During MCMV infection, m18 reduces phosphorylation of HDAC3 by directly interacting with CK2.
source: However, during MCMV infection, m18 reduces phosphorylation of HDAC3 by directly interacting with CK2 an activator of HDAC3.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: Many of the known HDAC inhibiting proteins from herpesviruses are crucial to viral fitness.
source: Many of the known HDAC inhibiting proteins from herpesviruses are crucial to viral fitness (Nevels et al., 2004; Gu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cellular HDAC enzymes have been shown to repress viral gene expression and, in some cases replication.
source: Cellular HDAC enzymes have been shown to repress viral gene expression and, in some cases replication.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HDAC function in viral infection.

claim: Chemical HDAC inhibition can rescue a defect in viral replication caused by HCMV IE1 deficiency.
source: In the context of lytic infection herpes viruses must overcome this repression using viral HDAC inhibitors (Nevels et al., 2004), in fact chemical HDAC inhibition can rescue a defect in viral replication caused by HCMV IE1 deficiency (Nevels et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: HDACs have been shown to occupy the promoters of the immediate early genes that drive reactivation in HCMV and MCMV.
